newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lawyer confident in Jones lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lawyer confident in Jones lawsuit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's attorney said on Tuesday it was "most unlikely" there would be an out-of-court settlement in the lawsuit filed by Paula Jones, but her lawyers appeared open to the idea.

Attorney Robert Bennett, commenting on the Supreme Court's unanimous ruling that Jones could proceed with her lawsuit, said he was "confident that the case ultimately will be resolved in the president's favour."
In a landmark decision, the nine-member court on Tuesday rejected Bennett's arguement that a sitting president should be given temporary immunity from civil lawsuits until after leaving office.
Jones accuses Clinton of making unwanted advances toward her in 1991 when he was governor of Arkansas and she was a state employee. Clinton denies the allegations.
The decision fuelled speculation that Clinton might settle the case out of court in order to avoid prolonging it any further, but Bennett seemed to dispel the speculation.
"The likelihood of a settlement is most unlikely because the president did nothing wrong," Bennett, said in an interview with CNN.

"The president denies the allegations of the complaint and has no recollection of ever meeting Paula Jones," Bennett said, adding, "I think that when all is said and done, the embarrassment will be on the side of Paula Jones."

Bennett stressed that Clinton "would never pay any money to settle this case" but did express a willingness to "issue a statement to the effect that what was written in the American Spectator never occurred."

Jones contends that she took the legal action to clear her name after American Spectator published an article claiming that Arkansas state policemen set up sexual liasons for Clinton. One of the women in the article was identified by the name "Paula". Jones alleged this tied her to the case.
Gilbert Davis, who represents Jones, told a news conference that the "the next move would have to come from our opponents" in terms of a settlement.

Insisting that his client was more concerned about clearing her reputation than in a cash settlement, Davis said that an agreement "came close to happening" before the current $700,000 lawsuit was filed but that it fell apart at the last minute.
"Our client, frankly, wanted to settle this matter without filing a lawsuit," Davis said. "She was perfectly happy to do so."

The Supreme Court ruling cast no judgments on the merits of Jones' case, but said it should be allowed to proceed. The case returns to a federal judge in Arkansas, where it has been pending since 1994.
"We thought we would get some sort of a mixed ruling ... but I am pleased with some of the language in the decision ... I'm not worried at all," Bennett said.
